primitives.name: Efferent Perception Precision
primitives.verbatim_quote: They admit of no great precision, and too much stress should not be laid upon them either way; but at the very least they tend to show that no added delicacy would accrue to our perception from the consciousness of the efferent process, even if it existed.
primitives.assumptions: Perception of efferent signals is imprecise and does not enhance sensory resolution.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When P_e approaches zero, consciousness of efferent process yields no additional perceptual detail.

layer2.mapping: GSI Bayesian model treats efferent signal as latent variable with low information content; GSE state transition uses impulse strength as control parameter.
layer2.telemetry: Variability in reported efferent sensation across subjects.

primitives.name: Motor Sensation Proportionality
primitives.verbatim_quote: This, however, is not the case, but the strength of the motor sensation is purely proportional to the strength of the impulse to movement, which starts from the central organ innervating the motor nerves.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'S_m': 'motor sensation strength (dimensionless)', 'I_c': 'impulse strength from central organ (dimensionless)', 'k': 'proportionality constant (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Motor sensation reflects central impulse, not mechanical work performed.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When I_c → 0, S_m → 0; implies no sensory feedback from muscle activity.

layer2.mapping: GSI inference links S_m to I_c via deterministic mapping; GSE models motor command execution using same kernel.
layer2.telemetry: Physician observations of altered muscular effects under pathological conditions.

primitives.name: Afferent Motor Feeling Hypothesis
primitives.verbatim_quote: Wundt says that were our motor feelings of an afferent nature, ...it ought to be expected that they would increase and diminish with the amount of outer or inner work actually effected in contraction.
primitives.assumptions: If motor feelings were afferent, they would reflect actual mechanical output.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When F_a ≠ f(W_{executed}), hypothesis fails; supports efferent origin of sensation.

layer2.mapping: GSI tests this via variance analysis of F_a vs. W_{executed}; GSE uses it to validate motor command fidelity.
layer2.telemetry: Comparison of motor sensation intensity against actual muscular effort.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core argument centers on the distinction between efferent and afferent processes in motor perception. The first primitive establishes that introspective awareness of efferent signals is inherently imprecise, implying that conscious perception of motor commands does not refine sensory resolution. The second primitive formalizes the relationship between motor sensation and central impulse strength, showing that sensation correlates directly with the initiating force rather than the outcome of action. This contradicts the afferent hypothesis, which posits that motor feelings should reflect executed work. The third primitive explicitly tests this hypothesis by proposing that afferent sensations would scale with mechanical output, yet empirical findings fail to support this. These primitives form a logical chain where the absence of afferent correlation validates the dominance of efferent signaling in motor awareness. Dualities emerge in the contrast between perceived effort and actual exertion, while failure modes arise from misattributing sensory feedback to mechanical work rather than neural drive. The epistemological structure reveals that perception of motor action is fundamentally rooted in central command rather than peripheral feedback.
